meta.framing: How do anthropologists adjudicate between rival interpretations of a burial site when one group reads the arrangement of remains as evidence of ritual practice and another reads it as the product of later disturbance?

response:
Disputes of this kind are adjudicated through depositional history rather than through competing intuitions about intention. Taphonomy is the study of the processes that affect human remains after death, and it furnishes the shared vocabulary in which two incompatible readings of the same arrangement can be made to compete for the same physical evidence. The procedure is to require each party to specify in advance what traces its preferred account would have left in the sediment, in the bones, and in their spatial relations, and then to look for those traces. The party invoking a deliberate act carries the heavier burden, since intentional interment is only one of several routes by which a body may come to lie in a depression in a cave floor.

The first line of argument concerns the spatial integrity of the skeleton. Articulation of adjacent skeletal elements indicates minimal post-depositional movement of a body, and that claim cannot stand together with taphonomy's being the study of the processes that affect human remains after death. Fully articulated skeletons, by contrast, are a diagnostic indicator of transport by flowing water. Whereas articulation points to a body that has scarcely shifted since it came to rest, burrowing animals can rearrange skeletal elements within a buried deposit, and taphonomy, the enterprise of tracing post-mortem process, is one specific instance of such rearrangement. In the contested assemblage, at least one bone was displaced from its original position after deposition, and that displacement is what conferred on the burrowers their power to shift elements within the matrix. At least one bone in the assemblage also lies in its original depositional position, and that claim cannot stand together with sediment micromorphology's being able to distinguish the fill of a dug pit from the surrounding natural deposit. At least one of those two descriptions holds of the assemblage, and perhaps both.

A second line of argument concerns the matrix rather than the bones. Sediment micromorphology can distinguish the fill of a dug pit from the surrounding natural deposit, which indicates that the sediment filling the proposed grave feature is indistinguishable from the surrounding cave floor deposit. Put differently, the fill of the proposed grave feature and the adjacent cave floor sediment have the same composition. Such a result constrains the excavator sharply: without a compositional or microstratigraphic boundary, the claim that a cavity was excavated and then backfilled rests on the outline of the feature alone, which is precisely the observation both parties already accept and interpret differently.

The discipline's own history shows these tests in operation. Pollen clusters recovered at Shanidar Cave were originally interpreted as the remains of flowers placed with a Neanderthal body, although rodent burrowing was later proposed as the mechanism that introduced the Shanidar pollen clusters into the deposit. A subsequent review of the Shanidar evidence determined that the pollen clusters were introduced by burrowing rodents rather than by mourners, and that determination settled the opposition between the floral reading and the faunal one by identifying which agent had in fact delivered the grains. Lee Berger and colleagues released preprints in 2023 arguing that Homo naledi deliberately buried its dead, an argument that came long after the original floral interpretation of the Shanidar pollen.

The Homo naledi remains from the Rising Star system are approximately two million years old, which places the funerary question at the far end of the hominin record and makes each associated detail consequential for the inference. Scrutiny has accordingly concentrated on what else the Dinaledi chamber yielded, since associated culture bears on whether the depositing agents were doing anything beyond falling or being washed into a chamber. Either no stone artefacts were recovered in association with the Dinaledi hominin remains, or at least one stone artefact was recovered in association with them; the two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. That unresolved point illustrates the general shape of such adjudication: it is not decided by which interpretation is more evocative, but by whether the specified traces of each proposed agent, cultural or geological, can be found in the deposit and distinguished from one another.
